channel.title: Methodic Truth — Chronicles & Changelog
channel.description: Field notes from building an AI agent from scratch, plus everything shipped on methodictruth.com, in the order it happened.

item.title: Changelog: September 5, 2026
item.description: No key on the Synth's keyboard is dead any more. The two-manual layout followed the piano strictly, and a piano has no black key between E and F or between B and C, which left a, f, k, apostrophe, 1, 4 and 8 doing nothing — two of them home-row keys. A dead key under resting fingers is a worse cost on a computer keyboard than a tidy metaphor is a benefit, so those slots now play the white note they lean against, which is not a fudge: E sharp is F and B sharp is C. So f plays F and k plays C. The range grew too: the three keys right of P continue the pattern, with bracket keys carrying the white row up to F and G and equals as the F sharp between them, taking the layout from two octaves and a third to two octaves and a fifth across 45 keys, both manuals still exact chromatic runs. A piano key that answers to several letters shows the main two and lists all of them on hover.

item.title: Changelog: September 4, 2026
item.description: The Synth's sequencer gets three fixes. On a phone the melodic grid and the drum grid were sized independently and were therefore two different scales stacked on each other: at 16 steps on a 390px screen, step 15 of the melody sat 151 pixels from step 15 of the kick, and the playhead lit two unrelated columns. They now share one scroller and identical column tracks, with zero drift at every width and length. Pitch now moves by scale degree instead of semitone — set a key and a scale, drag up or down on a step, and every edit lands in the key, with off-scale notes snapping in, Chromatic still available, and Random generating in your chosen key rather than always C pentatonic. And every step has velocity: melodic steps get a strip you drag, drum cells have no pitch so dragging up and down sets their velocity, which is where ghost notes come from, and the Beat preset lays hats with alternating accents rather than flat. Old patterns migrate to velocity 100, exactly what they already played at. The grid is also keyboard-reachable for the first time.

item.title: Changelog: September 3, 2026
item.description: The Synth now takes external gear. A new Audio In module puts a live signal from anything your computer can hear into the patch as a source — an interface with a guitar, bass or hardware synth on it, a USB mic, a drum machine, a turntable — and everything downstream treats it exactly like an oscillator, so the filter, delay, reverb, chorus and compressor all process your instrument and the LFO can sweep the filter while you play it. Echo cancellation, noise suppression and auto gain are switched off deliberately: they are voice-call processing, and on an instrument they gate off reverb tails, eat quiet passages and ride your dynamics away. A feedback guard cuts the input level if the master output pins for a sustained second, though headphones remain the actual answer. The interesting failure was silence: an Envelope is a note gate that sits shut until a key is pressed, so a continuous signal through one makes no sound at all, and the default patch has one — the module detects that, says so, and offers a one-click fix rather than routing around it, since the way round the envelope also skips the filter. Also: the computer keyboard now uses the whole keyboard. It followed Logic Pro before — seventeen keys, a tenth of range, two entire rows doing nothing. The default is now the tracker layout: your keyboard read as two pianos stacked an octave apart, one per pair of rows, with the black keys on the staggered row above sitting where they would sit on a real piano. That is 34 keys across two octaves and a third, enough for both hands at once without touching the octave control. Octave and velocity moved to the arrow keys so Z X C V are free to be notes. A layout menu restores the old Logic-style two-row map for anyone who has it in their fingers, and hand-made bindings are kept as Custom, so you can flip between a preset and your own map without losing either.

item.title: Changelog: August 21, 2026
item.description: New: the Harmony Workbench, a chord tool that draws the four voices instead of printing symbols and ranks its suggestions on voice leading it actually computes. With two guides: Writing Harmony (voice leading, borrowed chords, the lament bass, chromatic inner lines, and what Pieter Nooten does in Clan of Xymox) and The 4AD Sound (Blackwing, John Fryer, reverb printed as an instrument, guitar as texture, Vaughan Oliver). Also: DJing on the Prime GO+, the first DJ guide here — library prep and beatgrids in Engine DJ, cue systems, phrasing (sync solves the easy problem), EQ mixing, using stems without the artefacts, effects restraint, the energy arc, harmonic mixing, a gig checklist, and recording and releasing sets. Also new, Seeing the Fretboard: how good guitarists read the neck — intervals instead of note names, octave shapes as a navigation system (learn two strings and the shapes give you the rest), why the B string is the only irregularity on the instrument, position as a tone choice, triads on string sets, targeting chord tones, and what alternate tunings really change. The Synth also gets a real instrument on phones: touch pads, a grid of large multi-touch targets locked to a scale so there is no wrong pad, with rows offset two scale steps so three fingers stacked vertically make a chord, and sliding plays runs. Musical typing needs a keyboard a phone hasn't got, and the piano keys were narrower than a fingertip. Plus six new guides closing the biggest gaps in the education path. Space & Restraint turns "less is more" from a slogan into a method: why sparse music hits harder (attention is small, masking is physical, contrast needs a baseline), silence as something you play, dub as composition by deletion, eight techniques for taking things out, and the honest counterweight — empty and spacious are different things, and the fewer elements you have the better each one must be. Rhythm & Beats covers the note-level half of rhythm: what makes a beat good, ten load-bearing patterns drawn as sixteen-box grids (backbeat, four-on-the-floor, boom bap, trap, funk, one drop, tresillo, dembow, bossa, afrobeat), what every drum and percussion instrument is actually for, the techniques that make a part sound played, clave and polyrhythm, and nine exercises that need no instrument. The Mixing Guide — the word "panning" did not previously appear anywhere on this site — covers the static mix built with faders alone, gain staging, the low end, subtraction instead of EQ, automation, and how to listen in a room you can't trust. Groove & Timing: why perfectly quantized music sounds dead, and the three controls (velocity, placement, note length) that fix it. Choosing Sounds: the right sound needs no processing and the wrong one can't be processed into it. Finishing: the separate, teachable skill of getting a track to the end. Plus register conflict added to the Arrangement guide. And the Synth now wires itself: click Osc and you have a working instrument, and everything you add afterwards joins the signal path on its own — sources in parallel at the front, effects at the end, gaps closing when you delete. Order became the interesting decision instead of the tedious one, so every module got arrows to walk itself up and down the chain. The LFO gained a Drives menu listing every parameter in the rack, which is the first time modulation has been routable by hand at all — no cable can carry it. Hand-drawn cables are never re-routed. Plus: the computer keyboard breaks out of one octave with Z/X and fully remappable key bindings, and a four-voice drum machine on its own grid beneath the sequencer.

item.title: The Asset I Didn't Know I Had
item.description: Moving the Song Analyzer's backend off a cheap home PC into a $4 cloud VM looked like an obvious upgrade — faster CPU, real uptime, native Linux. The research reversed the decision. YouTube reads an IP's owner from public registry data, and a datacenter address is a high-signal prior for automation — inherited from whoever held that address last. The cloud plan meant paying for a VM, losing the residential IP, then paying again to rent one back. Also: the escalation ladder from attestation challenge to silent throttling, why proof-of-origin tokens stopped working, and a DNS outage that left a whole feature dark behind a green status light.

item.title: Changelog: July 29, 2026
item.description: A heavy week on the Synth: a filter with real teeth (drive, selectable slope, notch, self-oscillating resonance), an ADSR you shape by dragging its curve, drag-to-patch with compatible-port highlighting, five new presets, shareable patch links, and jam recording to a downloadable file. The Song Analyzer gained comprehensive analysis — meter detection, key confidence, song structure with an energy arc, and dynamics. Plus Sound Dispatches, a live music-tech news feed, and self-hosted fonts for faster loads.

item.title: Changelog: July 4, 2026
item.description: New Learn Production hub tying the guides into one visual, free path from a raw idea to a finished master, cross-linked record → arrange → mix → master. Plus a new Mastering Guide (the chain, loudness & LUFS targets, true-peak limiting, metering and the dithered bounce) and a Logic Pro reference (shortcuts, toolbox, and music-making features — Drummer, Flex Time & Pitch, Smart Tempo, quantize, Apple Loops, automation, Track Stacks, Live Loops). And housekeeping: removed pages now 301-redirect instead of 404, and static assets are cached at the edge for faster repeat loads.

item.title: Changelog: July 2, 2026
item.description: Three new visual guides for Logic Pro producers: a Recording Guide (microphones, polar patterns, placement, stereo miking, reamping, compression, punch-in/overdub), an Effects Guide (what every effect does, the signal-chain order, which effects pair together, and how to practice mixing), and an Arrangement Guide (song structure, the energy arc, and transitions, built with the Arrangement track). Plus: the Song Analyzer learns to live with YouTube's limits — paced/budgeted downloads, a browsable Library of instant replays, and a drag-and-drop upload path with no YouTube at all — and a site hygiene pass (full sitemap, canonical URLs everywhere, social cards, orphaned pages retired).

item.title: Stop Embedding What You Can't Control
item.description: YouTube's embedded player started demanding "confirm you're not a bot" from viewers — a check tied to their device, not our server. So the Song Analyzer dropped the embed and now plays the audio it already downloads, with a Web-Audio spectrum visualizer.

item.title: Changelog: June 30, 2026
item.description: Big Song Analyzer day: replaced the YouTube embed with self-hosted audio (killing the viewer bot-check) plus a spectrum visualizer; fixed the service-only stall and added a concurrency limit; added a live streaming progress bar, beat-synchronous chord detection (major/minor plus dominant- and minor-7th colors), shareable ?v= permalinks, and EBU R128 loudness normalization.

item.title: It Worked Everywhere Except Where It Ran
item.description: The Song Analyzer passed every test by hand and failed only through the installed service. The bug wasn't the code, the network, or YouTube — it was the worker's output pipe to journald applying backpressure and freezing the download mid-transfer.

item.title: Changelog: June 29, 2026
item.description: Added Song Analyzer and Fretboard to the Music nav dropdown. Fixed the gunicorn deployment on the physical Song Analyzer host (it was never actually installed). Made the host survive a real reboot — WSL2 auto-starts at Windows boot and the machine no longer sleeps. Added optional cookie support so yt-dlp can ride past YouTube's bot-check block.

item.title: What Real Hardware Costs You
item.description: A day after the Song Analyzer started doing real audio analysis on real hardware, that hardware proved it: gunicorn was never actually installed, WSL2 doesn't survive a Windows reboot on its own, and YouTube started blocking the requests outright.

item.title: Real Chords, Real Hardware
item.description: The Song Analyzer stopped faking it — a real audio-analysis pipeline now runs on a physical machine behind a Cloudflare Tunnel, hardened with caching, gunicorn, and a dedup lock.

item.title: Changelog: June 27, 2026
item.description: Added a searchable directory of every tool and page, a skip-to-content link and better keyboard support across the site, and the changelog. Filled in missing page descriptions and gave the site a proper 404 page. Moved the step sequencer into the synth itself. Made the ambient atmosphere calmer. Fixed the mobile hamburger nav dropdown. Added a Jam Guide, FM synthesis, an AI Dispatches feed, an Ear Training tool, a generalized Chord-Tone Trainer, a rhyme finder and syllable counter in Songwriter, a Rhythm Trainer drill, algorithmic chord voicings, and improved Theory piano legibility.

item.title: Changelog: June 26, 2026
item.description: Stopped the generative ambient music from autoplaying and hid the music player bar site-wide. Fixed the SPA router breaking onclick handlers on navigated pages.

item.description: How we built a free local AI inference tier across two machines — a gaming GPU and an Apple Silicon chip — and what it means to own your own compute.

item.description: Added the Song Analyzer — chord, key, and tempo detection from a YouTube link — connected it to a Cloudflare Worker backend, and gave it a dark, Byzantine aesthetic. Stabilized the synth's audio engine.
